title: The Binding of Isaac
overview: God tests Abraham by telling him to sacrifice his son Isaac, then stops him at the last moment, a story Jewish tradition calls the Akedah, meaning 'the binding'.

parts.label: A shocking test (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The reader is told this is a test, but Abraham is not. God asks for Isaac, the son Abraham waited decades for and the one God's promises rested on, as a burnt offering: killed and burned whole on an altar.

parts.label: The walk up the mountain (vv. 3-8)
parts.note: Abraham sets out early, and Isaac carries the wood up the hill, a detail Christians have long read as a picture of Jesus carrying his cross. Abraham tells the servants that he and the boy will return, and tells Isaac that God will provide the lamb; readers differ on whether he trusts God to spare or even raise Isaac, as a New Testament letter suggests, or simply cannot tell his son the truth.

parts.label: The knife is stopped (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: Abraham ties Isaac, lays him on the altar and takes the knife, until the angel of the LORD, a messenger who speaks with God's own voice, stops him. Many modern scholars read this as a rejection of child sacrifice, which some neighboring peoples practiced, though the text never says so outright.

parts.label: A ram in Isaac's place (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: Abraham sacrifices a ram caught in a bush in place of his son, and names the spot with a Hebrew phrase that can mean 'the LORD will see' or 'the LORD will provide', so translations and notes vary. The old saying tied to it, about the LORD's mountain, may point to Jerusalem's temple hill, which a later book calls Mount Moriah, but whether it is the same place is debated.

parts.label: A promise sworn (vv. 15-19)
parts.note: Because Abraham did not hold back his son, God swears by himself, since there is no one greater, and renews the promise of countless descendants through whom all nations will be blessed. The promise that they will possess their enemies' gate (some translations simply say cities) means taking those cities, since the gate was where a city was defended and ruled.

parts.label: News of Nahor's family (vv. 20-24)
parts.note: Abraham hears that his brother Nahor, back in the old homeland, has twelve sons: eight by his wife Milkah and four by Reumah, a concubine, meaning a wife of lower status. The list is here mainly to introduce Rebekah, Nahor's granddaughter, who will marry Isaac in chapter 24.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the chapter mainly holds up Abraham's obedience as a model of trust to be admired, or presents a deeply troubling command that readers are meant to wrestle with and question.
think: What would it take for you to trust someone enough to follow a request you could not understand, and where would you draw the line?
